$comment: The vocabulary this tool uses, defined once and read by both the visualiser (the Docs overlay and the Term popovers) and the CLI (`ambit help`), so the two can never drift apart. Ordered the way a reader meets them: everything on the map first, the terminal-only terms last. Every term here is the exact word the interface uses — src/client/vocabulary.test.ts fails if a surface starts calling one of them something else.

concepts.short: One thing your agent setup can do
concepts.long: Every MCP server, agent, skill, provider, model and command in your config becomes a capability. So do the nodes of the curated tech tree. A capability is the unit everything else is measured against.

concepts.short: How far up the tree a capability sits
concepts.long: The tech tree runs through seven eras: Foundation, Model Access, Tool Use, Memory, Autonomy, Assurance, Sovereignty. Later eras depend on earlier ones — you cannot run fully offline before you have a local runtime. Eras describe ordering, not importance.
concepts.seen: Column headers on the Tech Tree

concepts.short: Where you are on a tech tree node
concepts.long: Reached: something in your config provides this, and the graph records which capability proved it. Next step: prerequisites are met but nothing was detected — this is the useful frontier, and `ambit goal` lists it. Blocked: you have the tooling but a prerequisite is missing, e.g. retrieval configured with no vector store. Blocked is usually the most informative of the three.
concepts.seen: The three keys in the map legend, and the count in the header

concepts.short: Whether a dependency gates a capability, or only helps
concepts.long: A required prerequisite must be in place or the dependent capability cannot work — a model cannot run without its provider. An optional one strengthens something without gating it. Only required prerequisites block a node from being reached; both are drawn, with optional ones fainter. The data model and the CLI call these hard and soft.
concepts.seen: Solid vs dashed connection lines, keyed Required and Optional

concepts.short: A capability many others depend on
concepts.long: Ranked by how many capabilities would be affected if it disappeared. High-leverage to invest in, and risky to leave unmaintained. `ambit impact <id>` shows exactly what falls over. The map marks a node with three or more dependants; `ambit status` reports the same idea under the heading bottlenecks, counting only the combos a capability unlocks, so the two lists overlap without being identical.
concepts.seen: The dashed amber square on the map, and bottlenecks in ambit status

concepts.long: The tech tree nodes are combos, and you can define your own in a `combos` block for things specific to your work. A combo is a judgement about what composes into something new, which is why the tool never invents one from your config.
concepts.seen: The ● nodes and the Combos filter, ambit graph combos, ambit goal

concepts.short: A tool your agent can call
concepts.long: An MCP server, which is the protocol agents use to reach tools. Everything the server exposes — reading a file, opening a page, querying a database — becomes something the agent can do, which is why one server switched off can take a row of capabilities with it.
concepts.seen: The ◈ nodes, the Tool servers filter, and mcp entries in your config

concepts.short: Proven to work, not just configured
concepts.long: Detection proves a name appears in a config file. Verification runs a declared read-only check and records the result, so a capability can be said to work rather than to exist. Reliability is the share of recorded runs that passed, which is why the history is kept: one success is a weaker claim than forty-seven of fifty. Checks execute, so they live in the repository and run only when asked — never on seed.
concepts.seen: ambit verify, the evidence block in ambit status, and the map — a ✓ badge is a passing check, a ! badge is a failing one; a plain filled circle is configured but unproven

concepts.short: A 0-1 estimate of how established a capability is
concepts.long: Seeded from what kind of thing it is and whether it is enabled, then adjusted as your config changes. It is a rough ordering signal, not a measurement — treat a 0.8 as 'more settled than a 0.5', not as a score that means anything on its own.
concepts.seen: The ring around each node, and Maturity in the detail panel

concepts.short: The area of work a capability belongs to
concepts.long: infra, devops, backend, frontend, ai-ml, quality, security, or meta. Inferred from the capability's name, which means a stack unlike the keyword table's assumptions will land more things in the meta fallback — that table is the first thing to edit.
concepts.seen: Column grouping, and Domain in the detail panel

concepts.short: Time you spent stepping in so an agent could continue
concepts.long: Every recorded moment where a person had to step in — approve, correct, copy something across — priced at what an hour of your time is worth. The Attention lens shades the map by how often each capability demanded it; Time & cost ranks what removing it would save. Judgment and knowledge are never counted as reducible, however often they recur.
concepts.seen: The Attention lens, the Time & cost view, ambit attention

concepts.short: A change to your setup, drafted for a person to approve
concepts.long: An agent that finds a gap drafts a proposal rather than acting: the steps, their inverses, and what the frontier would look like afterwards. Approving it mints a signed artifact that expires; `ambit apply` verifies that signature before anything runs, and refuses if the proposal changed after approval.
concepts.seen: The Proposals panel, ambit propose / approve / apply

concepts.short: Whether it may run, not whether it can
concepts.long: Being technically able to perform an action is not permission to perform it. Authority is tracked separately per capability — observe and execute, each autonomous, confirm, or forbidden — so a reached capability can still require approval. This is what lets a larger technical surface stay governable: the limits are explicit rather than implied.

concepts.short: What the system can do, as of a moment
concepts.long: Every seed records the state of every capability, so the graph can answer what was reachable at a past date rather than only now. `ambit history since` compares two of those observations. Its useful column is the emergent one: capabilities that became reachable although nothing providing them was added, which happens when prerequisites are satisfied by something else entirely. A per-component changelog cannot show those, because no single change explains one.

`ambit decay` ranks capabilities by how long since their configuration last changed. It tracks configuration decisions, not how often you invoke something — a server you use daily but never reconfigure will look static, which is intentional. The question it answers is 'what have I stopped tending', not 'what do I use least'.
